intro: Use the present simple for habits, general facts and permanent situations: what you do every day, where you live, what you like. It is the tense you use most to talk about yourself.
objectifs: Use a verb in the present simple, with the -s for he / she / it and its spelling rules.
Make negatives and questions with do / does, and give short answers.
Know when to use the present simple: habits, facts, permanent situations, likes and opinions.

texte: In the present simple, the verb keeps its base form (the dictionary form, without “to”) with every subject except one: with he, she, it (and any singular subject like “my sister” or “the shop”), add -s.
This -s is the rule learners forget most. Remember: he / she / it → -s. “Have”, “do” and “go” are irregular with he / she / it: has, does, goes.
Most verbs just add -s. But some endings change the spelling, like plural nouns (lesson 12).

lignes: work → works, read → reads, play → plays
miss → misses, wash → washes, watch → watches, fix → fixes
study → studies, try → tries, carry → carries
play → plays, buy → buys, say → says

sections.note: “says” sounds like /sez/ and “does” like /dʌz/: the vowel changes when you speak.

sections.titre: Negatives and questions with do / does
texte: “To be” and “have got” don't need help, but a normal verb needs an auxiliary in negatives and questions: do (or does with he / she / it). The main verb goes back to its base form, without -s: “does” already shows he / she / it.
Negative: subject + don't / doesn't + base verb. Question: Do / Does + subject + base verb? Short answer: Yes, I do. / No, she doesn't. (Don't repeat the main verb.)
exemples: Do your children speak English? — Yes, they do.
What time does the train leave?
Wh- word + does + subject + base verb.
sections.note: “Do” can be an auxiliary and a main verb in the same sentence: What do you do? (= What is your job?), She doesn't do her homework.

sections.titre: When to use the present simple
texte: 1. Habits and routines, often with a time or frequency word: every day, every week, on Mondays, at the weekend, always, usually, often, sometimes, never (adverbs of frequency: lesson 7).
2. Facts and general truths: things that are always true.
3. Permanent or long situations: where you live, where you work.
4. Likes, opinions and states: like, love, hate, want, know, understand, think (= have an opinion), believe. Use these state verbs in the present simple even for now (lesson 9).
5. Timetables (trains, classes, films): The film starts at eight.
exemples: I get up at six every day.

texte: Some languages use one present tense for “I work” (habit) and “I am working” (now). English has two: the present simple for habits and permanent things (I work in Brussels), and the present continuous for what is happening now (I'm working now, lesson 8). Saying “I work” about this moment is a common mistake.

Also, English doesn't use the present simple for a period that started in the past and continues now: don't say “I live here since three years”. You will learn the right form at A2 / B1. For now, just remember: “since” and “for” + a period don't go with the present simple.

formule: I / you / we / they + verb · he / she / it + verb-s · don't / doesn't + verb · Do / Does + subject + verb?
prononciation: The final -s sounds like /s/ after p, t, k, f sounds: works /wɜːks/, stops, laughs.
It sounds like /z/ after a vowel or a voiced sound: lives /lɪvz/, plays /pleɪz/, reads /riːdz/.
It sounds like /ɪz/ (one extra syllable) after s, z, sh, ch, j, x sounds: watches /ˈwɒtʃɪz/, misses, washes, changes.
“does” /dʌz/, “says” /sez/ and “goes” /ɡəʊz/ have special vowels: don't say them the way they are written.
In questions, “do” and “does” are weak: Do you…? /də juː/, Does she…? /dəz ʃiː/. They are strong in short answers: Yes, I DO /duː/.
erreurs: After doesn't, use the base verb, no -s.
After does, use the base verb.
A normal verb needs don't / doesn't in the negative.
Do you like pizza? — Yes, I like.
The short answer uses do, not the main verb.
For an action happening now, use the present continuous (lesson 8).

dialogue.contexte: A journalist from a radio station in Yaoundé interviews a baker about her working day.
lignes: Good morning, Mrs Ngo. What time do you start work?
I start at four in the morning. I make the bread with my son.
Does your son work here every day?
No, he doesn't. He studies at university, so he only comes at the weekend.
And when does the shop open?
It opens at six and closes at seven in the evening.
Yes, I do! I love the smell of fresh bread, and my customers know me well.
Short answer; state verbs love and know.

exercices.consigne: Write the verb for he / she / it.
Put the verb in brackets in the present simple.
Write the sentence in the negative, then as a question.
items: He doesn't drink coffee. / Does he drink coffee?
You don't play the guitar. / Do you play the guitar?
Anna doesn't teach maths. / Does Anna teach maths?
They watch TV in the evening.
They don't watch TV in the evening. / Do they watch TV in the evening?

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Correct it.
items: Do you like rice? — Yes, I like.

exercices.consigne: Use the words to write a correct present simple sentence or question.
items: my father / not work / on Saturdays
My father doesn't work on Saturdays.
Do you speak English? — Yes, I do.

exercices.consigne: Describe a normal day in five sentences in the present simple: when you get up, work or studies, meals, evening. Add one sentence about a person in your family (he / she).
items: I get up at half past six. I take the bus to work and I start at eight. I have lunch with my colleagues. In the evening, I cook and I read. My wife works at home, so she doesn't take the bus.

a_retenir: He / she / it + verb-s (works, watches, studies, has, goes, does).
Negative: don't / doesn't + base verb. Question: Do / Does + subject + base verb? The -s moves to does.
Short answer: Yes, I do. / No, she doesn't.
Uses: habits, general truths, permanent situations, likes and states, timetables.
For an action happening now: present continuous (lesson 8), not present simple.
